transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I came in because I just can't stop thinking that the left side of my face looks off. It's like my nose and my jaw are crooked. I see it in every ID photo, or whenever I have my camera on for my online classes. 

Even when people tell me they don't see what I'm talking about, I just feel like everyone in the CNC lab where I work is noticing it. Like they're looking at my face before they even notice my programming or the actual work I'm doing. It's just really bothering me.
When you look in the mirror, are you mostly bothered by what you see on the left side of your face, or do you also feel unhappy with other parts of your body or your overall appearance?

No, it's pretty much just my face. I don't really have a problem with the rest of my body or anything like that. It's just... whenever I look in the mirror, my eyes go straight to that left side. The crookedness with my nose and jaw is all I can really focus on. So, yeah, I'm not unhappy with my overall body, just that specific part of my face.
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly, like checking mirrors, adjusting your face, or avoiding certain angles, to try to fix or hide what you see on the left side of your face?

Yeah, I do. Especially before I leave for school. I kind of get stuck just checking my face in the bathroom mirror, over and over. And then I'll pull out my phone camera to see how it looks on there, too. 

I try fixing my hair differently or changing my shirt a bunch of times to see if it helps hide the angle. I even end up asking my mom if my face looks weird before I go. It gets pretty bad, honestly... sometimes I do all of that for so long that I end up missing my lab completely. Or if I do finally make it in, I'm just too wiped out from stressing over it to even focus on my work.

Is your main concern that your face actually looks physically deformed or defective, even if others don’t see it, or is it more about how your face affects you in social or performance situations, like feeling distracted or embarrassed?

I mean, it's really the first one. I genuinely feel like it looks physically deformed. Even if my mom or other people say they don't see it, to me, it's just... it's physically crooked. 

The social stuff, like feeling embarrassed or being too distracted to do my programming at the lab, that only happens because I'm so focused on how messed up my face looks. So, yeah, the main concern is definitely that I believe it actually looks defective.
Does this concern about the left side of your face ever affect your mood, sleep, or relationships outside of work or school?

Yeah, it really does affect everything else. Like I mentioned before about missing my CNC labs, it's also making me miss my actual shop shifts. I just... I literally can't get myself out the door sometimes. It's gotten bad enough that my faculty mentor told me my work placement could be in jeopardy now. 

And as for outside of school and work, yeah, it definitely affects that too. I completely stopped playing soccer, and I used to volunteer, but I quit doing that as well. I just don't want people looking at me, so it's easier to just avoid all of it.
Have there been times when you're absolutely certain that your face looks deformed, even when you know logically that it might not be true?

I mean... I don't really know if I'd say I "know logically" it might not be true. To me, it just is true. I'm absolutely certain it looks deformed. Even when people tell me it's fine, I just think they're being nice or they aren't looking close enough. So, yeah, I'm always certain it looks that way, because that's just what I see.

latest_inference.note: The patient's persistent conviction that their face is physically deformed despite reassurance from others, along with the associated distress and functional impairment, strongly supports Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22). The patient explicitly denies any doubt about the perceived defect, ruling out disorders primarily characterized by doubts about appearance (e.g., as seen in delusional disorder, somatic type). No new disorder is added, and F44.5 is ruled out due to the absence of features consistent with conversion disorder.
